Let's talk about why the coin flip doesn't work.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There’s a really obvious problem with Survivor’s Coin Flip. The new game mechanic that was introduced last season gives one player a chance to double the prize pot and earn themselves an idol if they call a coin flip correctly or sends them home immediately if they don't. In theory, it's a high stakes game of chance that should make for exciting television, but there's an inherent structural issue that doesn't play well with network television.

The episode runtime spoiled the result of last night’s coin flip, just as it spoiled the result of Rick Devens’ coin flip on 50, just as it will likely spoil the results of any coin flip the show does in the future. Every episode ends with someone going home; so, if there’s a few minutes left when the person flips the coin, it’s bad news for them. If there’s enough time to do an entire vote after they flip the coin, it’s good news for them.

It’s an obvious problem and one that’s very valid for fans to complain about, but it’s actually not my biggest problem with the coin flip twist. I want it gone because it creates the potential to send someone home without being voted out.

Yes, sometimes people go home because they quit or get medically evacuated (get better soon, New England Rob), but that’s a natural byproduct of trying to survive in harsh conditions, not a production decision to try and generate drama. Yes, when there are four players left, we get a fire-making competition instead of a traditional vote, but that at least feels on brand to the show and also, is the subject of fan protests every single season. This coin flip thing, however, feels entirely different. It feels like a wacky gameshow element producers inserted because wouldn’t that make for fun television?

As a Survivor fan, however, I don’t think it makes for fun television. I am watching the show because I want to see the castaways actually play the social strategic game they signed up for. I want to see them try to navigate the island and their competitors and figure out how to survive each tribal council using the tools at their disposal. I don’t want to see one of them do an entirely luck-based challenge to decide their fate. That’s not the point of the game.

To be clear, luck does play a huge role on Survivor. Castaways go home all the time because they’re swapped onto the wrong tribe or their team loses an immunity challenge because other people blow a huge lead on a puzzle or whatever. The game is rarely fair, but in theory, even when it’s unfair, the player still has a chance to wiggle out of whatever danger they’re in. Get swapped onto a tribe against four members of an alliance? Try to find a crack and pit them against each other. Figure out that you’re on the wrong side of the numbers a few hours before tribal council? Go hunt for idols or make a fake idol or do something reckless to try and blow up someone else’s spot.

Those desperate shenanigans usually don’t work, but it still feels like the losing player’s fate was in their own hands. Maybe if they had found the right combination of words. Maybe if they had hunted in a different location. Maybe if they had built better relationships with the other side earlier in the game. Maybe if they had done something else, things would have been different.

You could look at the coin flip and say that’s an example of Survivor giving a player on the bottom a mechanism to change their fate, but to me, flipping a coin just feels so luck-based. It’s like a more obnoxious version of the Shot In The Dark, but at least with the Shot In The Dark, every player is given the same token and can use it in creative ways to build trust, try to avoid using an idol, etc. With the coin flip, it feels like a once a season game of chance for one player to do as part of a special event episode.

I didn’t like the coin flip when Rick Devens did it during 50. I didn’t like it last night when Lewis Kelly did it during 51, and I’m not going to like it next season when some unknown person flips it during 52. Yes, the runtime is an issue, but the bigger problem is it doesn’t feel authentic to the spirit of Survivor and the game they’re playing.

This season has been so good thus far. The characters are fantastic. The gameplay is chaotic. It's a great time, which is why I just want to see everyone play the actual show I signed up to watch.

#3948. Can GTA 6 make $2 billion in its opening weekend? One industry analyst has run the numbers, and seems to think so

We all know the story of GTA 5 making more than $1 billion in the first three days it was on sale, right? At the time, Take-Two believed this to be the fastest any entertainment property had achieved the impressive milestone - music and films included. It made history, and with ease. And it looks like GTA 6 is going to do even better.

At least, that's according to one analyst, Joost van Dreunen, a senior data analyst and great writer/numbers diviner who wrote some predictions in his respected SuperJoost PlayList newsletter. "My prediction: Take-Two announces opening-weekend sales above $2 billion by Monday, 23rd November," he wrote. And you know what? I reckon he's onto something.

Let's review what we already know: there is a conservative estimate of 10 million pre-orders for Rockstar's latest game floating around - something buoyed by comments from Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick - and, even by the company's lofty expectations, we know the game is tracking "well above expectations" when it comes to pre-orders.

We also know a lot of people are shelling out for the slightly more pricey Ultimate Edition (£90). So many people are opting for the more expensive version, in fact, that Take-Two revised its financial forecast up to $3.5bn for the next financial quarter, thanks to "recurrent consumer spending" (something Zelnick clarified in an investor's call is explicitly linked to the Ultimate Edition). 10 million pre-orders, at roughly $100 per copy - that's $1 billion right off the bat.

"That’s two days faster than its predecessor," van Dreunen said, "and largely before anyone has even played the game." That other $1bn will come over the weekend. And then, per the analyst, the game will sell roughly another 28 million copies over the course of the first year it's on sale. "My forecast puts first-year sales at 38 million copies, only modestly ahead of GTA 5’s 35 million. The real difference may be how much revenue each player generates over the years that follow."

But it's what follows in the newsletter that intrigues me most. "At the high end, [GTA 6] may just lift the entire industry with it," wrote van Dreunen. "In the face of AI slop and shitty mobile games that exist only to extract revenue, it will offer a reprieve. At a time when the industry is increasingly focused on making games cheaper and monetising players more aggressively, Rockstar is about to demonstrate the enduring appeal of spending a fortune to make something people actually want to play."

So, even if you're dubious about the game and Rockstar's motivations for selling as many copies as possible, the launch of GTA 6 could be something that gives the industry a much-needed jolt of life, in the face of rampant layoffs and shrinking talent pools.

It's not all sunshine and rainbows ahead for Rockstar, though: amongst the frenzy of launch activity, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week, as the game goes on sale.

#3945. Ever wanted to play a multiplayer version of Cyberpunk 2077 with your friends? Well, thanks to a mod now in beta, you can

You may have recently read that CD Projekt Red's in-development Cyberpunk 2 may be trying to revive the original game's online ambitions. But, if you don't want to wait the many years it'll likely be before the Cyberpunk 2077 sequel arrives, then I've got good news for you: Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP is now out in open beta.

"After almost six years of development, countless reworks, and code rewrites, we're finally launching the public beta," the modders on the CyberMP Discord channel wrote (thanks RPS). "Anyone can jump in and play now - no invites or applications needed." The team notes, however, that this is "true beta", meaning "Crashes, desyncs, and server drops under heavy load are completely normal for now. That's exactly why we need testers."

Alongside the potential shakiness, the devs say it's also possible the mod could ping your anti-virus software, since it "doesn't have a digital signature yet". Whilst the priorities for the team lie in "polishing the foundations" and "fixing crashes and stability", more features are eventually planned. But for now, they stress, "let's see how the project handles real player traffic!"

So, what exactly is it? CyberMP is a dedicated multiplayer modification for Cyberpunk 2077 that allows you and your friends to explore Night City together: drive vehicles, engage in combat, and play custom community-created game modes on high-tick dedicated servers. You need an official copy of the game to play it (obviously), and the mod is completely free to download. You can download the mod, and read a fair amount of how to get it working, what to expect from it, and how to troubleshoot any issues, over at its dedicated website.

If you're thinking 'Hang on, why does Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer sound so familiar?', it's because the game was supposed to receive an official multiplayer mode after its original release. Thanks to its shaky launch, however, plans changed, and CD Projekt Red later announced that multiplayer would be a separate "triple-A release", but, eventually, that too was cancelled. The studio is still keen to honour the idea, though, and recently stated it's "focusing on bringing online into all of our franchises one day".

This isn't the first big bit of news we've had about Cyberpunk 2077 mods this week. Just yesterday, a new mod called 'Torrent' added 3D rain, lightning storms, and tyre spray to Night City - all rendered and made lovely with a new lighting system that seems to play nicely with other weather mods that have been created for the game.

Their contributions were then double-confirmed by the full GTA 6 credits, which Rockstar published once launch time hit.

I’m the host of GTA 6’s “non-stop ‘80s” radio channel Vice City FM. I also wrote some in-game commercials, and I’m the voice of the Burger Shot ads as well! As a long-time fan of the Grand Theft Auto franchise, I couldn’t be more excited about this. Okay, gotta get back to playing the game!

"I’m the host of GTA 6’s 'non-stop ‘80s' radio channel Vice City FM. I also wrote some in-game commercials, and I’m the voice of the Burger Shot ads as well!" Yankovic said. "As a long-time fan of the Grand Theft Auto franchise, I couldn’t be more excited about this. Okay, gotta get back to playing the game!"

Somewhere out there, Weird Al is securing the love of his virtual latina wife, and I think that's beautiful.

Yankovic is just one of countless recognizable names you'll find if you scroll down the GTA 6 credits. Among the core cast, SNL alumnus Bobby Moynihan voices Cal, Jason's bumbling, conspiracy-brained buddy. The pair's criminal boss man, Brian Heder, is performed by legendary Stephen Root—who you'll likely recognize as Bill Dauterive on King of the Hill, Milton in Office Space, and all kinds of magnificent weirdos across the Coen brothers filmography.

But it's the radio talent where GTA 6's credits get particularly wild. It's a cavalcade of international music icons, comedians, and film figures. While driving around GTA 6, you might hear Lana Del Rey hosting Back Country Radio, or Latin music phenom Bad Bunny on Cocoteo FM. On Dirty South Classics, there's Trina, Trick Daddy, and Gucci Mane. Pop station Flash FM is helmed by Robyn and Alex Consani—the first transgender model to win Model of the Year at the British Fashion Awards and celebrated TikTok goofball. Keith Richards is in there. I didn't even know he was still capable of speech.

On talk radio, you can hear Ted Lasso's Jason Sudeikis, Abbot Elementary's Janelle James, and John Leguizamo of being John Leguizamo fame. Stavros Halkias is on there doing a Conservative talk radio bit. But maybe the most compelling inclusion, for me, is that Kaleidoscope FM is hosted by Jeremy Irons. The Academy Award-winning actor. You were in Kafka, Jeremy. How'd you end up in cyber-Florida?

#3943. GTA 6 hacker pleads guilty to 2022 Rockstar Games breach which the company claim cost them $5 million

Hacker was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital

A hacker has pleaded guilty to a number of online crimes, including the 2022 breach of Rockstar Games which resulted in a bunch of mid-development clips of GTA 6 in action leaking onto the net.

The BBC report that, on November 16th, Arion Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a number of others he carried out with the hacking gang Lapsus$ while aged 16 and 17. Kurtaj, now aged 21, was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital indefinitely due to the severity of his autism, but was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial. He'll be sentenced at a later date.

Kurtaj carried out the 2022 Rockstar hack while on bail for other hacking offences and being housed at a Travelodge hotel under police protection, the latter on account of rival hackers threatening to attack him over stolen Bitcoin stashes. The Rockstar hack was reportedly done using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into the hotel room's TV, plus a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

90 clips of unfinished GTA 6 were flung online by that hack, with Rockstar having refused to cooperate with Kurtaj's demand via an internal Slack channel that the company contact him on massaging app Telegram within 24 hours. Rockstar claimed the breach cost them $5m million to recover from, in addition to staff having to waste thousands of hours.

Earlier this year, GTA 6 suffered yet another leak, with a hacker or hackers going by "Cyberleek" posting various videos of the game in action. Rockstar and parent company Take-Two quickly sprung into action, taking down videos, filing subpoenas, and issuing a statement that called the leak "heartbreaking".

Hopefully with the game's console release later this week, those will be the only two GTA 6 leaks which have to be added to the annals of gaming history. As much as marketing can leave a bad taste in the mouth, especially when it barely shows anything of the actual product being advertised, neither of the GTA 6 leaks served much of a purpose beyond forcing people to waste some time and energy talking about the perpetrators.

#3942. World of Warcraft: Forever completionists push back as Blizzard gives them a powerful toy and then prepares to take it away

"Exactly the kind of FOMO that disheartens collectors."

With the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever there's a whole new world filled with niche gear and strange baubles to collect. But one item in particular has drawn the ire of the creators of a popular completionist add-on.

That add-on is All the Things, a must-install for collectors like me, as it acts as a database of all the gear, mounts, titles, crafting recipes, and super rare drops in the game. Once you collect something, it is hidden in the add-on, thus tracking your progress and making for a fantastic tool for picking the game apart.

On occasion, specific items have written notes attached by the All the Things development team, as is true of a special World of Warcraft: Forever toy, the Pouch of Violet Dust. This is a promotional item that was obtainable by watching two hours of WoW Forever streams between the 4th and 12th November.

It's a powerful toy! When used on a campfire, it changes the fire's colour to purple and extends the buffs provided by it from the usual one hour to two hours. But the sticking point with the item isn't its existence, rather the fact that it's going to be removed in early December, not long from now.

This is what the creators of the All the Things add-on don't like. "A week-long, Twitch-only window for an item that gets taken away a month later is exactly the kind of FOMO that disheartens collectors," the creators said in a note attached to the item in the mod. "It can't be earned by playing the game at all. Even those who get it don't get to keep it."

They aren't alone in feeling this way. Comments below the item's listing on the Wowhead database are equally scorching. "I love FOMO in their explicitly non-fomo game," wrote user TheWhiteRose.

"Just... Why?" added user Darrenic427. "They could very easily just patch out the camp buff duration and keep the visual effect, but Blizzard just doesn't like pretty fire I guess. Figures that they finally give us access to purple fire but then take it away after a month."

The battle between collectors and time-limited FOMO items is one that has been waged for about as long as these sorts of items have been a part of games. Though for the pouch, it's an especially weird case: an item that's cool to have but so temporary in nature that it makes it both important to completionists and strangely pointless to care about. Whether it makes a return in a later update for World of Warcraft: Forever and doesn't require out-of-game actions to obtain, and doesn't disappear, we'll have to wait and see.

WoW Forever itself is proving popular among players - me included. It's added a staggering amount of new quests and many new features to the original version of World of Warcraft, which, in turn, has injected the game with an impressive amount of new items to collect. Completionists will likely be glued to the game for a long time.

Some GTA 6 workout minigames such as the Kettlebell Swing are tricky to master, so here's how to make gains every time

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Knowing how to workout in GTA 6 will help you to increase your Strength and Cardio, which in turn will improve your health and increase your stamina. Working out will also manage your weight and build up muscle, affecting your appearance in GTA 6. While fancy gym memberships all over Leonida will become available in time, Jason has everything needed to get a sweat on right outside his house from the beginning of the story.

Realism is key here, so you can't just spend all day crunching weights as you'll soon hit a wall where no further gains can be made until you rest and recover – though consuming some protein after will halve the time you need to wait before you can go again. On screen prompts will inform you when you reach that point, and you can check the Fitness app on your phone to see what your current status and stats are. If you want to get fit fast, here's how to workout in GTA 6.

The lower deck area behind Jason's house is full of Strength workout equipment, so this is a great place to start building muscle. If you're still in the process of repairing the property, then this is also where to fix the railing in GTA 6. To start exercising with any of the equipment, walk up to it and follow the prompt.

Most of the Strength workouts in GTA 6 follow the same basic method – hold both triggers to lift the weight (or yourself), then gradually release the triggers to lower back down in a controlled way, before fully pushing in both trigger to repeat the process. You shouldn't rush this, but keep an eye on your stamina gauge in the top-left corner as if that fully depletes then your workout will end. You may also need to quickly press X/A to push out the last few difficult reps, so watch out for that prompt too.

Kettlebell swings in GTA 6 are not like the other Strength workouts, as instead of carefully lowering the weight you need to let it drop freely then start your next swing at just the right time to maintain the momentum into the following rep. Look for the point where the kettlebell is between your legs and almost as far back as it will go, then squeeze both triggers to swing it back up to the top again before letting go.

While most of the early GTA 6 workouts you can do at Jason's house are Strength-based, there is a way to build your Cardio here too. Head to the back of the workshop underneath the house and you'll see a HANG BAG prompt appear, so hold that button to set up your punching bag outside.

Unlike the Strength exercises that you have to interact with to begin, you can simply walk up to the punching bag and start pressing the Melee button to rain down hits on it. No progress bar or rep counter will appear, though you'll get a notification when your Cardio gains have been maxed out for the time being.

While this isn't a specific workout activity in GTA 6, you can also increase your Cardio by running or swimming for a period of time. A notification will appear to confirm this, but remember to check the Fitness app as if you've already maxed out your current Cardio gains then running all over the place won't give you further improvement.

As well as looking after your physical health, make sure you work on your GTA 6 relationship status to keep things sweet between Lucia and Jason.

It's been a thrilling week in movie news, largely thanks to confirmation that Robert Pattinson will be the next James Bond in Denis Villeneuve's developing blockbuster. Fans have been reacting to this news, but there's also been plenty of discourse about who might be joining the Twilight alum as the villain and/or the next Bond Girl. There are a number of fan choices swirling around online for the latter, and I'm glad folks are already asking these actresses if they'd be down to join the blockbuster.

The James Bond movies (which are streaming with an Amazon Prime subscription) have always had Bond girls. As such, we should expect some femme fatales to join Robert Pattinson in Villeneuve's developing movie. In a recent interview with Variety, actress Gemma Chan was asked about fans who want to see her in this role, responding with:

I’m flattered, and absolutely I would. It’s an iconic franchise, and I’m very excited that things are moving forward with it now.

We love to see it. Chan seems like a great choice to play a Bond girl, not only because she's a prominent British actress. She's also got plenty of action experience, thanks to her roles in both Eternals and Captain Marvel, as well as Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit. The latter doesn't feel far off from a 007 project, and the fact that she'd be down to join the 26th movie in the franchise is thrilling news.

Of course, there's no guarantee that the Five Star Weekend actress is actually being considered. What's more, there are plenty of other names that fans have been tossing around to play the next Bond girl.

Another popular choice from the fan casting perspective has been Sydney Sweeney, whose starpower has been growing for years. She's also trained in karate, kickboxing, and MMA, which could help her in any potential action sequences. Back in October of 2025, Variety asked the Euphoria actress if she'd be down to play a Bond Girl, and she responded with:

Depends on the script. I think I’d have more fun as James Bond.

This wasn't a yes, but it also wasn't a no. I have to wonder if her tune might have changed a year later, especially with Robert Pattinson now officially playing the martini-sipping MI6 agent. Either way, I have to assume that Denis Villeneuve has a number of actresses in mind to play a supporting presence in the 26th Bond movie. Hopefully we get more casting news sooner rather than later.

It's unclear when Bond 26 will hit theaters, but folks are assuming it'll be sometime in 2028. For now, fans can see Denis Villeneuve and Robert Pattinson's collaboration when Dune: Part Three hits theaters on December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list.

#3939. Intel are being sued for "misleading" investors about "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory" thanks to AI-fuelled price hikes

Tech giant Intel are being taken to court for allegedly "misleading" their investors about the sheer scale of the impact of generative AI-fuelled component price hikes on PC sales. The class action lawsuit in question claims that Intel's distribution and manufacturing partners have had to deal with "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", and that the gains from Intel's investments in AI datacenters aren't enough to make up for slowing sales of PCs to regular Josephines who just want fancy boxes they can play Deadlock on.

All this follows Intel's last round of quarterly results, in which they announced a significant revenue fall; this triggered an Intel stock price drop from $92.07 per share on October 29th to $65.76 per share the next day, which this week's lawsuit characterises as "the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years".

The lawyers in question are from Robbins LLP, who specialise in "shareholder, whistleblower, antitrust, & consumer litigation". In a press release, they say they've filed suit on behalf of anybody who bought Intel stock from July 23rd to October 29th this year.

The suit claims that Intel neglected to tell investors that falling PC and component sales were having a "materially greater negative impact" on their third financial quarter 2026 Client Computing and Physical AI Groupresults than Intel had previously stated – to the tune of "hundreds of millions of dollars" in revenue shrinkage, compared to the previous quarter, with the situation still expected to "worsen".

They also accuse the company of keeping schtum about the aforesaid "massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", together with the fact that "any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset by the negative effects on the Company’s business and financial results resulting from the PC market slowdown and the excess inventory buildup described above."

Finally, they say Intel bosses have failed to disclose that they're struggling to procure an adequate supply of substrates – that is, materials used to create the base layer of chips, circuit boards and similar components. As such, the lawyers claim, Intel couldn't "ramp up production to meet data center CPU demand even if the Company chose to divert production resources because of a slowdown in PC-related sales."

Once the Godzilla of personal computing, Intel haven't been having a brilliant few years. Back in 2024, they recorded a multi-billion dollar quarterly loss, pushing then-CEO Pat Gelsinger to resign. As regards sales of gaming PCs, they've fallen behind AMD, though they've reportedly taken some ground back recently as regards desktop CPUs. As regards graphics cards, they have long been dwarfed by Nvidia.

Any Intel investor who wants a piece of that lawsuit has until January 12th 2027 to sign up as a lead plaintiff – that is, a court appointee who represents the interests of other class members. As regards us little people who don't buy stock in huge technology corporations, all this merely continues the weird existential crisis wrought upon 'traditional' gaming and computing hardware by the feckless quest to sell a better chatbot.

#3938. UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is more worried "about the amount of time" people will spend on GTA 6 than the game's violent content

"I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter. I didn't hit anybody after playing those games."

Leader of the UK Conservative Party (and former Mortal Kombat player) Kemi Badenoch is more worried about the amount of time people will spend playing GTA 6 rather than the game itself.

Every new Grand Theft Auto game invites some amount of controversy over its in-game violence or depictions of sex and drugs - from San Andreas' raunchy Hot Coffee mini-game to GTA 5's graphic torture scene. Ahead of GTA 6's release this week, the Tory leader downplayed those fears.

"I would be more worried about the amount of time people were spending on a game than the game specifically. I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter. I didn't hit anybody after playing those games," Badenoch said in a news conference shared by Sky News (good spot, IGN).

While Badenoch's stance might be surprising for the normally right-wing UK political party, she did still worry over children who might play GTA 6 for too long. There are probably far worse ways for kids to spend their time than engaging with a long-form story like GTA 6's, though, especially in an era with endless amounts of 10-second clips to mindlessly scroll past and declining funding into youth programs.

"I haven't played Grand Theft Auto, I know people are worried about the game content. At the same time, I'd be more worried about a kid who played it all day, who was in their bedroom all day, than one who spends half an hour on it and then went out and did something else. They are two different things," Badenoch added.

GTA 6's release is imminent and is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time. One analyst even suggested GTA 6 could make over $2bn in its opening weekend - that's handily more money than Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey made during its entire run in cinemas, for context.

The game wears it surprisingly well, though we'll be less happy if the PC version is similarly capped.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For a bunch of performance snobs, we are a surprisingly forgiving bunch at PC Gamer. Yes, if you try to insult XCOM, you're going to get a slap, but we've only just started playing GTA 6 (well, some of us) and we're mostly over the whole 'only runs at 30 fps' thing already.

It turns out, while we're happy to part with our money to buy expensive components to hit higher frame rates (and earn the right to brag about it), we're also just as happy to settle for less when a game does a lot of other things exceptionally well.

GTA 6 certainly does that. That's the impression I get from most members of the team that have played it so far. Though if Rockstar is listening, when you do get around to our precious PC version, we'd love nothing more than 4K60—maybe more.

I will no doubt appreciate frames above 100 fps when GTA 6 comes to PC. Heck, I'd even just appreciate going up to 60 fps. But in my handful of hours with the game thus far, I just have simply not been that bothered by it. Be it smart ways of masking low frames, or even just the slower, methodical control approach of the game, I'm less frustrated with my PS5 running the game at around 30 fps than I was recently playing Phantom Blade Zero at well above 40 fps on a handheld PC.

Maybe that's down to the world having a little bit of magic to it, maybe it's the engrossing tone and atmosphere, maybe it's just because it looks so darn pretty. Maybe it's because I haven't got to the game's most hectic moments yet and haven't really needed to hit a headshot with my console unable to keep up with me. I'll tell you how I'm getting on in another fifty hours. Cool, see you in three days, then?

I was dreading playing GTA 6 on my OG PS5—a dusty ornament that's been chilling out in my living room this last year doing absolutely nothing. I've got a nice gaming PC in my office (RTX 4090, Intel i9 13900K, 32 GB RAM), so it's been a long time since I've had to deal with games dipping below 80 fps. I have been spoiled.

The second I got to control Lucia, my fears seemed justified. Everything just felt sluggish. But that feeling didn't last. I played GTA 6 for around 5 hours last night (I am very tired) and I haven't thought about the frame rate once since that initial section. Whether I'm getting into shootouts with coke smugglers, speeding through the Keys at night, or bouncing around at sea, GTA 6 looks great and feels great.

I can still tell this isn't 60 fps, but it is smooth.

I can still tell this isn't 60 fps, but it is smooth. I'm sure I've encountered drops, but crucially I haven't noticed them. Sure, it's inevitably going to look better and run better on PC, but the lower performance on my PS5 quickly ceased to be an issue, and I'm not regretting playing it on console.

GTA 6 is the kind of game where an uncapped framerate would be nice, but it doesn't feel essential. Like Red Dead Redemption 2 before it—a game I also played at 30 fps before it launched on PC—its pacing is measured. It feels designed around the limitations of the consoles it's launching on, prioritising detail and depth over twitch-based combat and precise interaction. It's exactly what I'd expect from a modern Rockstar game. Also like Red Dead Redemption 2 before it, I still feel the sense of longing for what this game will look like on PC. Make no mistake: the version currently available is a preview for what GTA 6 will be at its best. It's great, but those who can wait will be treated to a superior experience.

It's also possible that the 30 fps cap will feel more restrictive once the online mode arrives—whenever that will be, and in whatever form it takes. It's one thing to handle a lower framerate within Rockstar's meticulously created campaign. It's quite another in a lobby of other players. If GTA 6's multiplayer is even half as chaotic as the current GTA Online, every frame is going to count.

As I was booting up GTA 6, I was expecting to be annoyed by the game's paltry frame rate. And I was—at first. Much like Fraser, during the opening scene with Lucia, I saw my fears come to life on the big screen in front of me. Objects juddering and blurring as I swung my camera around in the cramped cell. Did I just waste £80 on GTA 6 on PS5 when I should've held my nerve for the PC version?

Truth is, the frame rate has had nowhere near as much of a negative impact on my experience while I've been traversing the Floridian wilds as Jason. In part, I think that's because there's a lot more going on, as cars, shops, people, and poultry fly past me as I break most state, federal and ethical laws. That reduces the chance of my eyes fixating on any one object and noticing the adverse effects of the game's lower fps, or the ways Rockstar has gone about covering for it.

Low fps is one thing, but motion blur is the devil.

Low fps is one thing, but motion blur is the devil. That's not just my opinion, that's been scientifically verified (sorta) to be the opinion of PC Gamer readers. Admittedly, some motion blur may be required when the frame rate is this low, so I have played around with a few settings in GTA 6 to find the perfect balance. I'd heard through the grapevine that higher-than-default motion blur (default is 3, goes up to 10) may be preferential to reduce the more obvious juddering that is present at low fps, but whoever says that is no friend of mine. I've landed on setting motion blur to 1 on the standard PS5, as it feels the cleanest overall. I wouldn't blame anyone for turning it off entirely, especially on a more powerful console where the frame rate may not dip as much.

Of course, I do agree with the rest of this lot: in an ideal world, playing the PC version, I'd be pushing a much higher frame rate with motion blur banished to the abyss where it belongs, and a full selection of graphics settings to tinker with to my liking. Yet, to my surprise, I'm not as much of a console version curmudgeon as I thought I'd be.

Is the low frame rate noticeable? Yep. Would it be better at a higher frame rate? Also yep. Is the low frame rate a detriment to my overall enjoyment of GTA 6? Only a smidge.

I don't consider myself much of a framerate snob, but I'll admit I was side-eyeing GTA 6's 30fps just a little bit. Well, that was before the game came out. Now that I have my hands on it, with roughly six hours spent lollygagging around Leonida? I'm hardly noticing it, though I'll most definitely be appreciating a smoother experience once the PC version rolls around.

Like Jacob said, motion blur definitely seems to be masking it somewhat—and I am traditionally a motion blur hater, so it's taken a little getting used to—but I'm genuinely pleasantly surprised at the balance Rockstar has managed to strike between a smooth performance and a dense, rich world.

GTA 6 taught me that I don't much care about frame rates as much as I expected. I got to start playing it a few weeks ago and didn't have anyone to compare notes with, and my first thought was: Huh, they got it to run at 60 fps after all! It all felt very smooth, even when I realized it was 30 fps after all. It was only a bit later I started noticing very occasional drops, like while driving during a gradual lighting chance from day to night.

But that's really infrequent. I think it being consistent is key. I'm on a PS5 Slim, by the way, not a Pro. That's not to say I still can't wait to see it at higher frame rates when it finally gets to PC. But 30 fps feels mostly fine for the time being.

It was actually spending a lot of time playing with handheld gaming PCs and laptops with integrated graphics that reminded me I shouldn't give as much of a shit about frame rate as I do. Largely that obsession is born of having high-end hardware sat in my desktop PC, but when crashing around with a range of handhelds I'm reminded of the old days when 30 fps was a target for PC games, too.

It's also reminded me that it really depends on the game engine, as well. Not every 30 fps game looks the same as other 30 fps games. And Rockstar has obviously worked incredibly hard to make sure that 30 fps looks as good as it possible can. Otherwise why would that be a solid target for all four of the console platforms it's released on?

For the most part Rockstar has done a great job of keeping things smooth.

I've been playing GTA 6 on the Xbox Series X, which does suffer from the odd dip in frame rate, too—though oddly I've only really noticed it during canned animations the characters do starting certain actions, such as opening the trunk of a car or pulling something out of it. But for the most part Rockstar has done a great job of keeping things smooth. And not just by using motion blur. For the record, I'm running that at 0 and have not looked back.

I'm less happy about the vignetting that I'm getting around the darkened edges of the screen, but I'm playing it blown up on a 4K projector so I've got plenty of screen real estate to enjoy. And I have been, thoroughly enjoying it, I mean. The frame rate, for me, hasn't got in the way once.

#3936. Each new GTA moves the series closer and closer to the original Mafia, the open-world game that bettered Rockstar

This week sees the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, the open-world crime 'em up that's been in development for at least eight years and has been waited on by fans for even longer. Naturally, over on PC we're still waiting for a port to be announced, let alone a release date to circle in our calendars. But, as happens whenever a new GTA is on the horizon, I think about Mafia: City of Lost Heaven.

Released less than a year after Grand Theft Auto 3, Mafia is perhaps a more prescient example of Rockstar's future than their own.

Set in Lost Heaven, a shoe-in for 1930s Chicago, Illinois, you play through Tommy Angelo's rise from a taxi driver, who has a chance run in with the Salieri crime family, to one of the gang's main enforcers in their fight against their rivals, the Morellos.

The influences on developers Illusion Softworks are obviously cinematic, with whole sequences ripped from The Godfather films and Goodfellas (and I'd argue there's a sprinkling of Once Upon A Time In America for good measure). A habit they share with Rockstar, who also pull liberally from crime films that share the settings of their games. But Illusion Softworks are also clearly interested in capturing the history of the Prohibition era, too. The story begins in the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street Crash and the depression that followed, running through until the late 30s, and you see that time pass in the city around you. Buildings that are under construction at the start of the game are completed by its end, a used car lot in Chinatown sits empty for most of the game until business picks up with the economy, but most enjoyable of all is that the cars driving the streets change. At first the roads are filled with Ford Model-T-inspired vehicles that basically look like horse carriages with engines, but by the end of the game they've all become much sleeker creatures that have left their early carriage influences behind.

The city Illusion Softworks built also has a dedication to verisimilitude that we see Rockstar adopting in their later games. As you drive Lost Heaven's streets, you must pay attention to speed limits and red lights, as speeding and running traffic lights will both earn you a fine if a policeman spots you. For fans of public transport, there are streetcars and overhead trams you can ride to navigate the city, too. Two other touches I love: when you reload your gun, you dump the whole clip instead of returning the unfired bullets to a magic ammo reservoir, and vehicles can run out of fuel if you drive them too far.

Much had been made of all the simulations running under the surface of Grand Theft Auto 6, such as fully realised cloud formation, a smell reaction system, and… fuel tanks that can run empty. No doubt they're significantly more impressive than what's on show in Mafia, and this isn't about putting the two games against each other (even if one of them was likely made for less than the other studio spent on coffee runs across its eight-year development). Nor is it about saying history recognised the wrong game: Grand Theft Auto 3 was a huge step forward in open-world gaming and Mafia was recognised and celebrated in its time. It's about something else.

Back in 2002, Illusion Softworks offered a different kind of open-world crime game. One that was more mature despite having a lower age rating. Grand Theft Auto was undoubtedly more influential, sparking imitators that mostly opted to follow its tone and sensibilities – Saints Row began in a similar place to GTA 3 and as the series continued leaned further into the silliness and parody, for instance. But while for many years Mafia stood as a sign to an open world path that could have been taken, the longer Grand Theft Auto series has gone on, the more Rockstar have found their way toward the example set by Illusion Softworks. The games are still aiming for bombastic comedy at times, but they're also interested in the likes of newly-arrived-in-America Niko Belic, or Michael de Santa, a retired criminal haunted by his past. They're much richer protagonists than Claude, the silent character you play in GTA 3.

The Mafia series has continued, marked by ideas that remain as interesting as what was on show in the original. In Mafia 3, you play Lincoln Clay, a black soldier returned from the war in Vietnam and brought into the family. Set in a take on New Orleans, Louisiana, during the civil rights movement, you face overt racism. Linger too long in white, wealthy neighbourhoods and the residents will call on the police to move you along. And the Definitive Edition remake of the first game, released in 2020, is a rare example of a game that both captures the spirit of the original and justifies its existence by expanding and bettering the story. Though I don't think any of its sequels have been as innovative, nor as forward thinking, as the first game.

I don't want to come across as Rockstar-bashing. The studio have continued to push the open-world genre forward with every release and I want to see what other developers lift from GTA 6 for their own games. But I'm even more pleased that as the studio's aged, their work has grown closer to Illusion Softworks'.

Kirk in Grand Theft Auto 6 is out to hunt bigfoot, or the Skunk Ape, or Mr. Mangrove, depending on who's talking about it

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Bigfoot in GTA 6, also known as Skunk Ape or Mr Mangrove, isn't just an Easter egg, but a full blown chain of side quests tied to a character called Kirk, who's obsessively hunting the cryptid through the Floridian swamp. After your character stumbles across Bigfoot's location, you can contact Kirk and help him hunt down the Skunk Ape for good across several missions, in which you find the strange effigies that this creature is leaving behind. All this wraps up with a fairly significant choice, one that harkens back somewhat to the famous bigfoot encounter in Red Dead Redemption.

To start with you'll have to ensure your random encounter with the Skunk Ape, but afterwards you can pursue the quest line pretty straightforwardly. Pick the right choices, and you can get a real cash reward.

For a friendlier form of wildlife, check out how to pet animals in GTA 6.

The Skunk Ape questline in which you help Kirk hunt down a monster he calls "Mister Mangrove" is broken up into several smaller quests and objectives.

This is a questline you can start very early on in GTA 6, all the way in chapter 1 1, and see through to the end in the same chapter. The rewards are pretty significant, assuming you make a certain choice.

To find Bigfoot initially in GTA 6 before starting the Skunk Ape quest, you need to go to the location on the GTA 6 map marked above. Once there, you'll see Bigfoot moving fleeing into the marshland after eating a deer.

It's not mandatory that you follow (or even that you have this encounter for the larger quest), but if you do, you'll be led to an effigy tied to a tree. Examining it for too long causes you to inhale spores from it and pass out.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

To start Kirk's quest "Skunk Apeology 101", go to the Rusty Anchor bar in North Key Lento. On entering through the main doors, look immediately to the right and examine the notice board. There'll be a poster left by Kirk, with a number to call if you've seen the Skunk Ape.

With the number added to your contacts, call Kirk. He'll give you a meeting place and time to start the quest, marked on your map with KK.

Meeting with Kirk and getting some explanatory dialogue, he'll have you hit a stick against a truck to trigger the distant howls of Mr. Mangrove. You'll follow him into the woods (I recommend you equip your flashlight in the equipment tab in the bottom left radial menu).

To find Mr. Mangrove after splitting up, use your Focus Mode when you hear the Skunk Ape howling, and there'll be a ripple effect. Follow those ripples until a chase is triggered, leading to another effigy.

At this point, after studying it, you'll be chased by a strange boar. Don't worry too much about escape – whether it catches you or not, you'll end up back at the car, either because you flee successfully or because you're knocked out and Kirk drags you there. He'll tell you he'll contact you again with the next steps, which will take about half a day in-game.

Kirk tells you that he needs you to find three tree Effigies left behind by Mr. Mangrove. There are actually nine of them in total, but you only need to find three of them. We've marked all their locations on the map above – when you're close, use Focus Mode again to see them through the trees, then use L2/LT to study them.

After completing this, you'll be given another message to wait, as now Kirk has the data needed to track the Skunk Ape down for good.

On meeting back up with Kirk at night, you'll be given a customised tranquilizer rifle and taken up in a helicopter. After flushing out the Skunk Ape, you need to fire several rounds into it. Despite the long range, there's no drop-off or delay on the rifle, so just aim at Mr. Mangrove's centre mass and you should be fine.

Eventually he'll end up in a small encampment. Follow him into the building, and you'll see him pass out. When you try to lift him however, things get weird, as you'll be exposed to the pollen spores he emanates and pass out.

In this questionably hallucinatory experience, you'll now control a frog and have to find flies to eat. There are three different spots to go to where flies congregate over corpses.

Be wary that there are alligators who will try to eat you. Keep your distance, and use Focus Mode to home in on the flies.

Having eaten flies, now you'll become one, obviously. Head back to the shack you found the Skunk Ape in, but now follow the other pier around back to the helicopter (its lights should mark it out). Stay close to Kirk, and you'll hear him talking about a man named Harry Sherrick who disappeared – who actually is Mr. Mangrove, with a valuable QR code tattoo that will lead to open his substantial bank account.

Waking up in the shack with Kirk and the unconscious Mr. Mangrove, you can choose to side with either of them, now knowing that Kirk is fully aware that the Skunk Ape is some transformed human being and is only hunting him to rob him. You can choose to shoot either of them with the dart gun, or neither. Here are the options and what they give you:

No matter what outcome you pick, you get to keep the rifle, a legendary variant "Mister Mangrove" Laird 350 Bolt Action Rifle. That reward, at least, is consistent.

Of the three, the best choice if you want to make money fast in GTA 6 is to shoot Mr. Mangrove. However, if you want to be an ethical criminal, I would shoot neither and let the Skunk Ape have his revenge.

It's heavily implied that Mr. Mangrove is a man named Harry Sherrick who was transformed by swamp spores into a Skunk Ape, similar to the mutated boar that chases you early in the quest chain.

Kirk knows this and has been relentlessly hunting and hounding Sherrick anyway – not to help him, or to reveal the truth to the world, but to simply get access to the tattoo and steal the money. Kirk's a pretty shitty person, simply put, especially as he had no intention of even cutting Jason and Lucia in on the reward.

If you lose track of your new rifle, make sure you know how to store and recover your weapons in GTA 6.

#3934. Original GTA 6 leaker pleads guilty to hacking Rockstar Games, years after first revealing Lucia

The 21-year-old responsible for hacking Rockstar Games and leaking in-development GTA 6 footage in 2022 has pleaded guilty to a number of offenses.

The GTA 6 leaker was initially sentenced to an indefinite stay at a hospital due to his severe autism, but was more recently deemed fit for trial and moved to a regular prison earlier this January. On Monday, at the Woolwich Crown Court in South East London, he pleaded guilty to hacking Rockstar Games and a number of other companies, including Uber and EE/BT, in cyber attacks estimated to have caused £10m in damages.

At the time of his Rockstar hack - when he was between the ages of 16 and 17 - the leaker was already under police protection at a Travelodge hotel to keep him from rival hackers he had allegedly stolen Bitcoin from. Somewhat surprisingly, he then managed to hack the multi-billion dollar game maker with nothing but an Amazon Fire Stick, the hotel room's TV and a bluetooth-connected keyboard and mouse.

As the BBC reports, he also managed to break into the developer's Slack channels, before threatening to release the GTA 6 source code if Rockstar failed to contact him within the day. The leaker has yet to be sentenced.

Those 2022 leaks were quite substantial, too, revealing about an hour of unfinished gameplay and clueing the world in on Lucia's existence - the series' first female protagonist in years. Of course, those 2022 leaks shouldn't be confused with 2026's, which saw Cyberleek spill nuggets of nearly finished clips onto the internet, despite Rockstar's best efforts to keep GTA 6 a closely guarded secret.

"We recently suffered a network intrusion in which an unauthorised third-party illegally accessed and downloaded confidential information from our systems, including early development footage for the next Grand Theft Auto," Rockstar said at the time, before it had officially unveiled GTA 6. "At this time we do not anticipate any disruption to our live game services, nor any long-term effect on the development of our ongoing projects. We are extremely disappointed to have any details of our next game shared with you all in this way."

Four years later, GTA 6 is finally around the corner - you're probably already aware considering the marketing frenzy Rockstar's been drumming up.

#3933. My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

Longing for the Venetian Dogehouse, stuck in the Venetian doghouse

The tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east. Yet, I still can’t reach out and grasp the throne that sits right in front of me. I’m Marco Sanudo, and the throne of the serene republic of Venice eludes me.

I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less. I’ve managed to avoid punishment for that crime, despite the fact it earned me a fiefdom to rule while I’ve tried to up my patrician score enough to be the lucky party the next time a ruling Doge dies in office (or runs out their 10 year term). Sadly, Doge Leonardo, the mysterious masked lord who’s had an iron grip on power since the first couple of old blokes to hold the position in this playthrough popped their clogs, is proving incredibly tough to oust.

It should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast. It certainly did in being granted a pardon for offing that other Marco, but not even that and a plague which infected nearly everyone in the realm aside from me have paved the way to Dogedom. In the meantime, I’ve striven to gain wealth and influence. I’ve worked up to having four trade routes running at once, with goods like wine, iron, and textiles flowing from market to market across southern Europe and bringing a steady supply of coin back to my Venetian estate. I’ve built trade posts at the extremities of my routes, giving me the option of starting from further afield and reaching new lands if the cash flow dries up closer to home.

This is where Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion has blended a bit with the game’s traditional feudal moneymaking to supercharge my coffers. The land holding I killed a dude for, the Proveditorate of Zara, means I’ve also had tax money from modern day Croatia to add to both my trade profits and the income my domicile generates on its own. I am, as the medieval kids say, minted.

Getting to the point of serious pocket clinkage is, as you might imagine given Silk and Silver’s focus on filling the game’s world with travelling merchant companies and wheeler-dealing republican patrician families, the beating heart of the expansion. A near-constant stream of notifications about prices of different goods I’m trying to hawk in different locations encourage me to regularly prune and re-work my routes so that max profits are being earned and no carrying capacity’s being wasted. The bubbling up of wars and plagues impacts prices in affected cities, making it a never-ending battle if you’re desperate to optimise everything within an inch of its life. I’ve found that degree of micromanagement unnecessary if the goal is just to keep a decent profit margin ticking over. Just remember to replace the trader assigned to a route if they die, recall them every few years so they don’t stress themselves to death, and check in every so often to re-evaluate whether you’re running goods that are suitably in demand.

If you stick at it for a decent amount of time, with a certain type of good - alcohol or jewellery, for example - your expertise in dealing in them increases, making it easier to sell for better prices. Trade routes left running between the same markets also gain boons from being in place for a long time, offering a counterpoint to rejigging them every five seconds to wring out a few more coins. Most of my routes have run along a path that includes stops at four markets, with the occasional location boasting a monopoly I’ve bargained for with the local ruler, so I don’t have to worry about competition at every stop.

When you’re playing as a merchant who isn’t locked into the ruling inner circle of a republic, making your routes as lengthy as possible is one of the three moneymaking areas your company can specialise in. That first one’s caravaneering, and is the one I leant into in a non-Marco Sanudo playthrough. Beyond that, you can become an expert loan shark, lending cash to rulers or paying their ransoms in order to recoup interest and collect hooks you can use for favours. Manufacturing expensive artifacts that can be sold individually to collectors for a profit is the third option. The latter two I’ve only dabbled in a little bit as of writing, having earned enough gold mostly from caravanneering to buy the land containing the city with my home market and be anointed a Sheikh. So, beginning as a landless merchant is a nice alternative to Crusader Kings 3’s long-established wandering adventurer starting point, with both allowing you to work your way up from lowly serf to landed lordly dynasty in your location of choice.

If you’re after a more specific historical scenario, Silk and Silver has Guelphs and Ghibellines. This is where we find Marco Sanudo, as well as the other patrician family head I’ve played as thus far, Speronella Dalesmanni. The setup is that the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor have had a bit of a tiff, essentially rooted in who should have certain powers, with different cities and powerful families in northern Italy taking either the Guelph (Pope-likers) or Ghibelline (Holy Roman Empire-enjoyers) side depending on what suits their goals or principles. I’ll be honest, aside from being another way to easily earn friends or enemies in the ruthless crucible of merchant republican politics, where votes and reputation-bolstering aid from other nobles are key, the situation’s not had a hugely obvious bearing on my playthroughs thus far.

I think the closest it’s come is during my Dalesmanni run, if largely due to the existence of the By God Alone expansion allowing a new branch of Catholicism, dubbed Italian Christianity, to be created. The initial conversion push from the bishop responsible led a number of my fellow northern Italian nobles away from the Roman Rite headed by his Popeliness, making the Guelph/Ghibelline split more clearly defined.

In the early hours of both my Sanudo and Dalesmanni playthroughs, I’ve been far more focused on simply trying to push the respective patrician families up the hill from posh toffs with naught but a vote and a manor to elected rulers of their great cities, with land holdings to match. Speronella’s situation in Padua is made incredibly tough by the fact she’s a woman in a world where every succession rule is designed to put blokes first, so I’ve had more success with Marco and his quest to become the Doge of Venice.

As the head of a patrician family, one of select few elite clans who steer the oligarchical republic, I was faced with earning Marco enough respect among his fellow family heads that they’d consider voting him to the top of the succession list, thus securing his power whenever the current Doge got the boot. Pulling that off, while also not kowtowing to the requests and schemes of those same peers, isn’t easy. A large cocktail of factors go into determining whether another noble likes you enough to vote in support of your succession. There’s your patrician rating, which is upped by doing things which specifically show you to be good at this Italian noble house lark, such as establishing trade monopolies for the republic, gaining the Pope’s favour, or having close relatives who also hold key positions in the republic. However, how close a friendship you have with the target and how their character traits align with you also play a huge rule.

Thus it was that, at one point, Marco was best mates with the current Doge and had a decent patrician rating, but had only amassed 68 of the 72 points needed for said Doge to vote for him because the Doge was generous, and therefore didn’t care for Marco’s ambitiousness. That same Doge either liked or respected Marco enough to grant him a council position and the status of regent, but he would not back Marco to replace him permanently for love nor money. This is the same man who liked Marco so much that when I pulled off that not-so-sneaky murder on another noble house head in order to inherit the keys to the Proveditorate of Zara, the Doge was instantly willing to pardon me and prevent Marco suffering any punishment for the crime.

Not even a couple of serious plagues hitting Venice, which at one point had all three people ahead of Marco in the queue suffering from smallpox, could get him on that throne. Eventually, it took a bit of lucky timing when his Doge mate died of old age - a few years after beating smallpox - to finally install Marco as Doge. Given that delayed promotion, as of writing I’ve not yet had enough time in the big chair to give a proper verdict on how it differs from regular feudal rulerdom in the long run.

What I can do instead is tell you a bit about the fun of council votes. The same pool of voters who in a republic like Venice, get a say in who succeeds the ruler, also vote on the passage of laws and decrees. One proposal you can put forward is a vote to change who exactly is allowed a seat in this voting pool. It defaults to just being heads of patrician families, but can be extended to include all vassals, or tightened up so only the Doge’s councillors or the ruler themselves have a say, that being the way despotism lies. As you can imagine, passing a change to who can vote can drastically change the state of play, either tightening up the number of folks who might oppose or support you, or bringing new folks into play in a fashion that dilutes individual power, but gives you more pieces on the board to mind or manipulate to your advantage.

I’ve found it suitably tough to orchestrate successful votes to change laws and customs which medieval Italian noble families, expectedly, have firmly entrenched stances on. Getting rid of checks and balances, such as the requirement to vote on banishments or wars - so the Doge can rule as a despot - has proven one such challenge, as has changing laws governing men being prioritised over women. I tried to pass equal succession as a substitute for men being put first while playing as Speronella, but met an insurmountable wall of resistance due to the region’s culture and faith. So, all I could do was try to put my young male heir in the best position possible to make the sorts of gains I couldn’t.

Much easier to weasel into place, either through some canny swaying or the offering of hooks, are laws giving state backing or other priority to trading in certain types of goods. Alcohol, for instance, which certainly hasn’t hurt the profits of Marco’s two wine trade routes.

Thus, cash continues to flow through the tentacles of my trade empire in sizable globs. As he’s now Doge, I’ve got Marco using the ample funds of Venice’s treasury to build a new piazza and have him focused on making the city’s already-strong trade league even more formidable, by attracting new members from the few other northern Italian blocs.

While I’m fairly sure there are folks who’ll find Silk and Silver's constant barrage of trade route notifications annoying, or that their power-grabbing skills and sheer multitude of money-making means combine to make playthroughs less challenging than they could be, so far I've found it another enjoyably sonorous string to Crusader Kings 3’s bow. Above all else, playing as a merchant gives more reason to invest in stewardship skills beyond just maximising your tax yields, while the republican politics of the DLC's main region fleshes out rewarding intrigue-focused builds. Diplomacy and martial skills are less key, but still have their place at times.

If you’re an absolute stickler for historical accuracy, you may well find other things to gripe about, but aside from the Guelph and Ghibelline conflict fading into the background, I’ve found plenty to like in my quest to become top Doge.

I've been playing GTA 6 through the morning to try to see what the fuss is about, and now I totally get it. After mere hours in the game, I'm already coming to terms with the scale of it; not just the size of the map, but the attention to detail on every object and interaction. But I have to remind myself, this is sure to be the worst version of GTA 6 we'll ever play.

That sounds like an insult, but I mean the exact opposite. If this is where the game is at launch, at its most barebones, running on years-old consoles on their way out, then think of what it will be like at its peak.

I work for PC Gamer, so forgive my snobbery when I say the PC version should be far superior to what we're currently playing on consoles.

A part of that is the possible frame rate bump from running on modern PC hardware. The standard PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S/X are powered by pretty outdated architectures by today's standards: RDNA 2 and Zen 2. You're looking at the Radeon RX 6000 series and Ryzen 3000 series for PC equivalents.

These chips have recently received support for more modern ML-powered FSR upscaling techniques from AMD, though Rockstar has only seen fit to enable FSR 4 on the Xbox Series S to help the underpowered console along. Sony also has AMD-powered upscaling tech for the PS5 Pro, but the standard PS5 doesn't get a whiff of that.

It's only really the PS5 Pro with a more modern GPU—loosely equivalent to an RX 7800 XT—that might temper expectations for how fast the game may run on a modern gaming PC. Rockstar has said the PlayStation 5 Pro wouldn't be capable of a steady 60 fps even with the more powerful hardware compared to the base model; however, hints at the sluggish CPU as perhaps the weak link. The PS5 Pro runs the same old eight-core CPU as the standard PS5, and if Rockstar's engine can make use of faster, more multithreaded CPUs with lots of cache, we should see a performance bump on PC.

That's not to exclude older gaming PCs. The Xbox Series S can cope with GTA 6, so should many gaming PCs of all levels. Notably so if Rockstar offers a range of upscaling options.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

It's ubiquitous upscaling that should make an even bigger difference to an eventual PC release and performance on all manner of PC. We know the game supports FSR 4.1, as both Sony and Microsoft are already using this as the foundation for their upscaling technologies on console, and Red Dead Redemption 2 offers both FSR and DLSS on PC. Since that game's release, we've seen the advent of frame generation technologies from both AMD and Nvidia, which could further increase how smooth GTA 6 feels on PC.

As a serial settings tweaker, I've been sorely disappointed by the sliders, or lack thereof, available to me in GTA 6 on the base PS5. I want levels to this stuff; an advanced menu for advanced men like me. I want to manage the foliage detail, draw distance, and ray-traced effects. Speaking of which, I'm sure we'll have the option to enable ray-traced shadows, currently exclusive to the PS5 Pro, and crank up the quality of most effects in the game on PC.

The non-RT shadows are one of the few noticeable drawbacks about the standard PS5 version of GTA 6 I'm currently playing. They can pop in and out from reflections, and there is a jagginess to them in places.

Is any game going to be modded more than GTA 6? Our Joshua has been busy modding GTA 5 to try to turn it alchemy-like into GTA 6 for months now, and he never ran out of mods to install. While he may have strayed from his original mission almost immediately, the message is clear: GTA 6 is going to have a seriously busy mod scene.

The game will be all the better for it, too. Not every mod is going to enable a roving band of militant furries (Joshua's words, and no need to mod those into GTA 6) or trap the player in a tiny car; I'm sure GTA 6 will actually be a better game for the efforts of modders. It just takes a PC version and some intrepid people to make it happen.

This one is easy; one of the reasons for GTA 5's long-lasting legacy is the combination of GTA Online and custom jobs via the creator. Neither of which are actually here for GTA 6 yet. So on a very basic level, and you don't have to be a PC gamer to agree on this point, GTA 6 is going to get a lot better for the eventual online mode. And there will be an online mode, right? Even if Rockstar hasn't technically announced one is on the way yet.

On the flipside, if you're constantly getting griefed by a guy that only plays GTA 6 all day and won't let you leave your house in GTA Online, perhaps you could argue the game was better when it was single-player only.

It pains me to admit it, but GTA 6 is not only going to eventually run better on PC. It might be the definitive version in my eyes, but console gamers do have a high-fidelity future ahead of them, too. Both Sony and Microsoft are planning new consoles that seem pretty likely to come out in roughly a year's time—providing the memory crisis doesn't ruin everything—and AMD is set to be providing more powerful silicon for these systems.

We're expecting to see the RDNA 5 architecture make its way into the next-gen consoles, paired with Zen 6 CPU cores of some size and description (these may be heterogeneous). That would put the consoles on a level playing field with PC components likely to launch around the same time (Zen 6 should be available on desktop by then, while perhaps a more limited launch for RDNA 5 by early 2028).

So that whole spiel about how current-gen consoles are years behind our fancy PCs won't get me so far once these new systems come out. I'll have to find a new stick to bash consoles with… er, not enough RGB LEDs? Anyways, the definitive GTA 6 experience on console is still yet to come—that'll be the version that's ready to make the most of these more capable units sometime next year or in 2028.

There are going to be a helluva lot of patches, upgrades, and DLCs to come for GTA 6. Remember, GTA V got a new first-person mode with the then-next-gen PS4 and Xbox One, so there's plenty of opportunity for genuine upgrades down the line.

Though, saying that, by recent PC standards (poor ports, game-breaking bugs, and more), this GTA 6 launch has been relatively issue-free. I mean, I've seen a couple of visual glitches and my colleagues have had some strange men falling out of the sky, but besides those open-world oddities you may expect of a game of this size and stature, it's been pretty smooth sailing so far.

I just hope the PC version can claim a similarly clean sweep for its eventual launch. So far, no word on when that might be.

#3930. Spirit Crossing, the new Zelda-ish hangout MMO from the creators of Cozy Grove, understands that sometimes you just want to be alone

New multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five. By default, players appear to each other as shadows, all exploring a skybound landscape of magic animals and layer-cake mountains that reminds me of both Sable and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

Deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities. For example, going fishing, playing instruments round the campfire, playing dress-up and pulling emotes in group photos, bouncing around on strangely inflated yaks, or questing forth to heal troubled spirits. There's some material gathering and crafting, and there are recurring storms that make the ambience more threatening, but overcoming a challenge doesn't feel like the point of Spirit Crossing. The "missions" are just an excuse to hang out together.

There's nothing forcing you to do any of this in company, mind. "Stay a mysterious shadow, lend a hand when you feel like it, and disappear before anyone can make it weird," the devs explain, adding a hug emoji to make plain that they don't think you're some kind of smelly misanthrope for shunning other players.

I, personally, am a smelly misanthrope, and will only ever appear in your game as a skulking opacity, peering through the window of your personal gingerbread house, with its tastefully accessorised lava lamps and throw rugs. No, I will not join you for a group hang-glider tour. No, I do not want to play the banjo with you. You will experience me only as the nagging sensation of being watched, while you chat to the local "Stylesmith" about fetching rucksack patterns.

Spirit Crossing has an upfront cost that "gives players full access to the complete game experience in perpetuity", but you can also take out a subscription for some cosmetic items and access to a "limited resource exchange shop". They're avoiding traditional microtransactions, which is nice.

Spry Fox are also the developers of Cozy Grove - "the best grove since Byker", wrote Graham, in one of his regular 'senior moments'. I myself know them as the studio behind wintry puzzler Road Not Taken, with its randomised woodlands, and block-merging city builder Triple Town, with its unexpectedly terrifying bears. Little about Spirit Crossing seems terrifying, unless you count the shadow loitering at the edge of your conversation pit.

You can read more about the game on Steam. I find Spirit Crossing quite novel, especially when it dispenses with the WholeCosy "discover your inner fashonista" stuff and leans into the supernatural elements: I like the idea of hunkering by the campfire during a storm, watching the clouds hurtle past. Still, I'm disappointed to hear that Spry Fox have made use of generative AI during its creation.

As has been pointed out to us on Bluesky, the developers called on Anthropic's Claude tools for various behind-the-scenes tasks - the example they give in a Discord post is editing several config files at once. There's no disclosure on the game's Steam page because Spry Fox haven't used AI tools to generate any of the art or music - Valve rewrote Steam's disclosure requirements in January to exempt the usage of generative AI for "efficiency gains", which the above presumably falls under.

It's hardly a full-throated endorsement of generative AI, but it still forms part of a political and cultural project I consider reckless and morbid. For a longer account of my objections, albeit one that doesn't cover Claude in particular, here's my longform thinkywangle from July last year.

#3929. Star Wars: Galactic Racer is getting much-requested split-screen multiplayer and new mode in 2027

The surprisingly awesome arcade podracing game Star Wars: Galactic Racer is getting split-screen multiplayer next year after loud fan requests, developer Fuse Games has announced.

Split-screen racing comes as part of an entirely new mode called Free Play that'll also allow players to mix and match vehicles, characters, tracks and planets in a galaxy far, far away. So, maybe don't expect to bring friends into the game's vast, pre-existing suite of modes just yet.

"We heard you," the studio wrote on social media. "Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at Fuse Games has been working hard to bring a brand new mode, Free Play, to Star Wars: Galactic Racer. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action."

We’ve heard you! Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at @Fuse_Games has been working hard to bring a brand new mode, Free Play, to STAR WARS: Galactic Racer™. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action.

Galactic Racer already has a pretty good selection of online multiplayer modes, like the 12-player speeder races and 8-player podracing tours, but there's currently no way to play with your mates in the same room.

Chris Donlan loved the thrilling racing game for mixing the best bits of Star Wars and Burnout - Fuse Games does have plenty of old Criterion DNA, mind you. "It's new games, with Roguelite choices and endless unlockables, and it's also old games, with cruel and ingenious courses where everything can be lost in an instant. It's a Galaxy Far, Far Away, and it's also Paradise City," he wrote in Eurogamer's five-star review.

With Galactic Racer and Zero Company under its belt, Lucasfilm Games said it's now "more flexible" about which developers it accepts pitches from. Hopefully, that'll lead to even more interesting games set in Star Wars' ultra flexible world.
